ChannelFormer: a Transformer-based model for fNIRS missing-channel reconstruction

From quality control in paediatric ASD brain-imaging data to an idea for EEG bad-channel reconstruction

Presenter  ·  Haozhi Wang
Zhao Y, Li K, Cao Y, Chen Y
Applied Soft Computing · Vol. 195, 2026 · 115032 · DOI 10.1016/j.asoc.2026.115032

Why this paper: aggressive bad-channel rejection in our ASD EEG recordings leaves too many interpolated channels. This paper asks the same question in fNIRS — can a lost channel be rebuilt from the channels that survived?

03 / 12
Interpolation TodayThe method we currently use

How spherical spline interpolation fills a bad channel

The setting

International 10–20 system (Wikimedia) — our case: F3 bad, the rest usable

Core assumption: the scalp potential field \( V(\mathbf{r}, t) \) is a spatially smooth function on the scalp sphere — F3 is not unrelated to its neighbours.

$$ \hat{V}(\mathbf{r}_0, t) \;=\; c_0(t) \;+\; \sum_{i=1}^{N} c_i(t)\, g(\cos\theta_{i0}) $$

r₀ position of the bad electrode  ·  i the remaining good electrodes  ·  θₐ₀ spherical angle between electrode i and the bad site  ·  g(·) spherical spline kernel  ·  cᵢ(t) coefficients solved from all good electrodes at each time point

Not a neighbour average

\( F_3 \;\neq\; \tfrac{1}{4}\,(\,Fp1 + F7 + Fz + C3\,) \)

And not inverse-distance weighting either — a smooth field is fitted through all electrodes’ spatial relations on the sphere.

Repeated at every time point

t = 1 ms  all good electrodes → solve cᵢ(t) → F̂3
t = 2 ms  repeat → F̂3
…
↓
whole series  F̂3(t)
What it actually uses: electrode geometry + the instantaneous spatial potential field. No training, no learned \( P(F_3 \mid F_7, F_z, C_3, \ldots) \) from large data — it is model-based spatial interpolation, not data-driven reconstruction.
04 / 12
Core IdeaChannelFormer · 2026

Treat channels as tokens

Familiar: NLP Transformer
I↓token
love↓token
EEG↓token

Attention asks: which other tokens should each token look at?

⇆
Here: ChannelFormer
CH1↓token
CH2↓token
CH3↓token
CH4↓token
…↓…
CH50↓token

A time slice of the channel = the token’s feature. Temporal points are features, not tokens.

1 channel = 1 token
its time series = token feature

With \( C = 50 \) channels and slice length \( T \), the input is \( X \in \mathbb{R}^{50 \times T} \) — fundamentally different from time-step-as-token Transformers.

Why this reframing is the whole point

  • What is lost is an entire variable, not a few noisy points — a dead channel removes a whole column of the data matrix.
  • The 50 channels are not independent: the scalp field is smooth, so neighbours constrain the gap — exactly what attention can exploit.
  • Time goes into features, not tokens: tokens stay few but long, matching fNIRS’s slow dynamics.
05 / 12
MechanismChannelFormer · 2026

What does self-attention actually do here?

The general rule
$$ \mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) \;=\; \mathrm{softmax}\!\left( \frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) V $$

No need to memorise it — it computes weighted relationships between every pair of tokens. Here, the tokens are channels.

Applied to one lost channel — same relationship, drawn
\( \widehat{CH}_{17} \;\approx\; \)\( 0.30\, CH_{4} \)  +  \( 0.20\, CH_{18} \)  +  \( 0.15\, CH_{23} \)  +  \( \cdots \)

The weights in the equation are the labelled arrows above — one relationship, two views. (Not literally a linear blend; it is the intuition that holds.)

Multi-head = different relationship types

Head 1 → nearby channels Head 2 → global co-fluctuation Head 3 → other dependencies
⚠ \( \text{attention weight} \neq \text{functional connectivity} \)

Model attention is a computational mixture — it must not be read as a neurophysiological connection.

Design DetailsChannelFormer · 2026

Three key designs, in plain words

① Binary mask — “tell the model what is real”

Every channel gets a tag: 1 = really measured, 0 = missing, please invent it. The model never has to guess which channels it should trust.

1 bad ch.11111011111 several110101011001 1 source1111001100111

Third row is the realistic one: one light source feeds several channels — if its scalp contact fails, CH5, CH6, CH10, CH11 vanish together, not at random.

② Time slicing — “cut long records into short windows”

A 2-min series is far too long to feed in as one feature. So each channel’s record is cut into short windows; each window becomes one token’s feature.

Fig. 4 (paper) — correlation vs. patch length
shorter features
less overfitting
more training windows

fNIRS signals barely carry long-range temporal dependencies, so little information is lost by cutting.

③ Hybrid loss — “values right and shape right”

MAE alone can be gamed by a flat average: numbers close, dynamics gone. So the reconstruction is graded on two things at once:

$$ L \;\sim\; L_{\mathrm{MAE}} \;+\; \lambda\,\bigl(1 - r\bigr) $$
MAEare the values close to the original?
rdoes the reconstructed wave rise and fall in the same places?

ResultsChannelFormer · 2026

How well does it recover 12 missing channels?

Correlation coefficientTDASD
Single-channel loss0.8226 ± 0.00320.7024 ± 0.0025
12-channel loss0.8022 ± 0.00180.6719 ± 0.0026
Light-source loss0.7953 ± 0.08040.6689 ± 0.0849

Source: ChannelFormer, Applied Soft Computing 2026

Fig. 5–7 (paper) — original vs. reconstructed ΔHbO, one scenario per table row

Phenomenon 1. Losing 24% of channels doesn’t collapse performance

TD 0.823 → 0.802, ASD 0.702 → 0.672: even with 12/50 channels gone, waveform correlation stays moderately high. fNIRS channels carry substantial shared information — cross-channel reconstruction is viable.

Phenomenon 2. ASD is consistently below TD

TD r ≈ 0.80 vs ASD r ≈ 0.67–0.70. Candidate causes: (1) more movement / lower SNR; (2) more heterogeneous neural signals. But this result alone cannot decide which — AI does not remove the raw data-quality problem.

Critical QuestionChannelFormer · 2026

Is ChannelFormer simply better than spline? Not so fast.

1 · Needs no training data at all

pop_interp(EEG, chan, 'spherical') works immediately — no 1000 subjects, no train/val/test split, no GPU. ChannelFormer first needs large amounts of complete, high-quality data as ground truth, artificially masked so the model can learn \( X_{\mathrm{masked}} \rightarrow X_{\mathrm{complete}} \).

2 · Generalizes naturally

It depends on electrode coordinates, not a training distribution — ASD, TDC, ADHD, adults, children: any reasonable montage works. ChannelFormer risks domain shift: trained on awake TDC, tested on chloral-hydrate-sleep ASD means \( P_{\mathrm{train}}(\mathrm{EEG}) \neq P_{\mathrm{test}}(\mathrm{EEG}) \) — a real warning for our data.

3 · Injects no cohort prior

An ASD-specific ChannelFormer could bake training-cohort priors into \( \hat{X}_{\mathrm{bad}} \); asking “ASD vs TDC?” on that reconstructed data then becomes circular. Spline learns no labels and injects no population prior — it does not manufacture an ASD prior.

11 / 12
Take-Home MessageChannelFormer · 2026

Three things to remember

1

ChannelFormer turns complete channel loss into a cross-channel reconstruction problem: \( CH_{i} \sim P(CH_{i} \mid CH_{1}, \ldots, CH_{i-1}, CH_{i+1}, \ldots) \).

2

Channel-as-token + self-attention learns global cross-channel dependencies — performance holds even with 24% of channels missing.

3

For our ASD-EEG work: bad-channel handling itself deserves systematic validation — the reconstruction method may shape the biomarkers we report.

Can learned EEG reconstruction preserve physiological biomarkers?
